newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's PRI ahead in peaceful state election.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's PRI ahead in peaceful state election.

text.p: Mexico's ruling party took an early lead in local elections in southwestern Guerrero state in largely peaceful voting that could help end a recent wave of armed violence.
While early returns showed the Institutional Revolutionary Party on track to win most town halls, the PRI may have lost much ground to the leftist Democratic Revolution Party (PRD).

With only five percent of the vote counted, the PRD was narrowly ahead in the resort city of Acapulco, the state's most populous city, and was also winning in the state's third city of Iguala. The PRI was ahead in the state capital Chilpancingo and in nearly every race for the state congress.
PRD leaders said their returns showed them winning by less than one hundred votes in Acapulco with 25 percent of the vote tallied and also ahead in fourteen of the 76 other town races.
"I think we have great news," Manuel Lopez Obrador, the charismatic new leader of the leftist party, told reporters early on Monday in announcing the results.

Lopez Obrador said it was too early to call the election fair, but he said the vote was peaceful and praised the Mexican army and armed rebels of the Popular Revolutionary Party (EPR) for not interfering in the poll.

Troops were ordered to suspend their counter-insurgency operations against the newly-emerged EPR and stay in their barracks for the day. EPR rebels also suspended attacks on the army during the election.

Acting state Gov Angel Aguirre called the elections an unprecedented step for democracy in Guerrero, a dirt-poor state plagued by political violence that has given rise to several guerrilla movements over the years.
The PRD complained before the election that PRI was using dirty tricks to gain votes and vowed to reject any outcome it considers to be the result of fraud.

Fears of violence may have kept many voters at home. PRI officials estimated half of registered voters stayed away from the polls, but independent electoral observers said the figure was closer to 60 percent.

A PRD electoral observer was stabbed to death early on Sunday in the town of Altamirano, some 150 miles (260 kms) north of Chilpancingo. But State Attorney General Antonio Hernandez Diaz said he believed the incident was not related to the elections.
Shaved voter lists, vote buying and voter intimidation were reported in some parts of the state, according to Alianza Civica, an election watchdog group that had some 300 observers across the state.
The PRI, which has ruled Mexico for 67 years, has historically held overwhelming political power in the state, controlling 68 of the 76 town halls.
Early returns showed no major gain for the conservative National Action Party, which has gained support in other parts of Mexico due to an economic crisis and government corruption.
